summary: Gives an overview of the protocol suite for real-time communication in browsers (WebRTC), meant as a starting point to find all required parts.

eli5.summary: A map showing all the pieces that let a web page do video calls.

subtitle: A roadmap listing which specifications a browser or device must implement for real-time audio, video and data.

tldr.problem: Real-time audio and video in browsers needs many protocols, and without one list implementers could not tell which parts they must support to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8825 is an applicability statement: it specifies no protocol itself, but groups the needed functions and says which other specifications a WebRTC endpoint MUST implement for each group.
tldr.outcome: It is the starting point for finding every part of the WebRTC suite. It is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC replacing or updating it.

today: RFC 8825 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It stays the roadmap whose referenced documents define what WebRTC endpoints implement.

sections.title: Why a Roadmap for Browser Real-Time
sections.content:
The Internet was long seen as a vehicle for real-time, interactive applications such as Internet telephony and video conferencing. Early attempts needed special networks, special hardware and custom-built software. As bandwidth and processors improved, a satisfactory experience became possible on commonly available computing hardware.

Two barriers remained: there was no single set of communication protocols that everyone agreed to make available, and no universal identification system like telephone numbers or email addresses. Meanwhile the browser-embedded web application had become a platform, and HTML5 promised to offer the needed interfaces in a standard way instead of through separately installed plugins.

This memo describes building blocks that can be exposed through a JavaScript API and together allow interactive audio and video between browsers across the Internet. The goal is to cover the required scenarios in the WebRTC use cases document, RFC 7478.
sections.eli5: Phone calls used to need special equipment. Now a web page can do it, but everyone first has to agree on the same set of rules.

sections.title: Goals, API and Protocol
sections.content:
The document is an applicability statement. It does not specify any protocol itself, but says which other specifications implementations must follow to be compliant with WebRTC. It defines shared terms and points to the other documents of the suite, so that reading it and the documents it refers to should give all the information needed to build a WebRTC-compatible implementation.

The total WebRTC effort has two parts: a protocol specification done in the IETF, and a JavaScript API specification defined in W3C documents. The protocol specification does not assume that every implementation has the API, so a peer does not need to know whether the other side is a browser. The aim is that each protocol option maps to clear API calls and the reverse.

The RFC distinguishes a WebRTC browser (conforms to both protocol and API), a WebRTC non-browser (protocol only), and a WebRTC-compatible endpoint (can communicate with WebRTC endpoints but may miss some requirements). A data channel is an abstraction for sending messages between endpoints, and two endpoints can have several.
sections.eli5: There are two rulebooks: one for how computers talk to each other, and one for what buttons a web page gets to press. This RFC points at both.

sections.title: Interoperability and a Mandatory Baseline
sections.content:
Internet communication usually has two phases: the parties work out what functionality they both support, then use what they share, or give up if nothing is common. The RFC stresses that a mandatory-to-implement function set exists to prevent negotiation failure, not to prevent negotiation.

With such a baseline you can communicate as long as you conform and the other side accepts the base level. Without one, you must implement the standard "and then some", usually a profile, which in its worst form means using one vendor's product only.
sections.eli5: If everyone agrees to know at least one common language, any two people can talk, even if they also know other languages.

sections.title: Architecture and Functionality Groups
sections.content:
The model does not assume the browser contains every function of a telephone or video conference. The browser supplies functions for a web application that works with its backend servers. That makes two interfaces vital: the protocols browsers use to talk to each other without intervening servers, and the APIs offered to JavaScript.

The commonly imagined deployment is the browser RTC trapezoid. The media path goes directly between the browsers, so it must conform to the WebRTC protocol suite. The signaling path goes via web servers, which can modify, translate or manipulate the signals. If the two servers belong to different operators, the signaling between them must be agreed by standardization or other means, for example SIP or XMPP. These choices are outside the scope of the suite.

The RFC splits the needed functions into six groups:

  • Data transport: TCP and UDP, secure connection setup, congestion management, bandwidth estimation.
  • Data framing: RTP, SCTP, DTLS and their confidentiality and integrity functions.
  • Data formats: codecs and format specifications.
  • Connection management: setting up connections and agreeing on formats, such as SDP, SIP and Jingle/XMPP.
  • Presentation and control: floor control, screen layout and similar cooperation functions.
  • Local system support functions: things like echo cancellation that need not be uniform on the wire.

The first three form a media transport infrastructure and the last three a media service; for interoperable services at least the first five groups need to be specified.
sections.eli5: A video call is built in layers, like a sandwich: moving the bits, wrapping them safely, choosing the picture and sound format, setting up the call, and little helper jobs on your own machine.

sections.title: What an Endpoint MUST Implement
sections.content:
The core of the RFC is a list of required specifications, one group at a time.

  • Transport: the protocols in RFC 8835, including congestion control, retransmission and in-order delivery.
  • Framing and securing: media travels in RTP (RFC 3550), and SRTP (RFC 3711) is REQUIRED. Endpoints MUST implement RFC 8834, RFC 8826 and RFC 8827, plus the data channel specifications RFC 8831 and RFC 8832.
  • Data formats: endpoints that support audio or video MUST implement the codecs and profiles in RFC 7874 and RFC 7742.
  • Connection management: WebRTC browsers MUST implement RFC 8829 (JSEP). All endpoints MUST implement its network-layer functions such as BUNDLE (RFC 8843), rtcp-mux (RFC 5761) and Trickle ICE (RFC 8838), without needing its API parts.
  • Presentation and control: WebRTC browsers MUST implement the W3C peer connection and media capture APIs.
  • Local functions: endpoints MUST implement the processing functions in RFC 7874.
sections.eli5: It is a shopping list: for each part of the call, it names the exact other documents you must follow.

sections.title: Connection Management Principles
sections.content:
Setting up, negotiating and tearing down connections is a large subject where both interoperability and freedom to innovate matter. Three principles apply:

  1. WebRTC media negotiation can represent the same SDP offer/answer semantics (RFC 3264) used in SIP, so a signaling gateway between SIP and WebRTC can be built.
  2. Legacy SIP devices that support ICE and appropriate RTP and SDP mechanisms, codecs and security can be gatewayed without a media gateway, though a signaling gateway may be needed.
  3. When an SDP for a new codec is specified, no other standardization should be needed to use it in browsers, and old applications should be able to use it with no JavaScript changes.

The RFC also notes for operators that WebRTC session setup typically happens over TLS-secured web technologies with application-specific protocols. Techniques that insert network elements to interpret SDP, such as SIP ALGs, will not work with it.
sections.eli5: Setting up a call is like agreeing on how to talk. The rules let web calls and old phone systems understand each other, and let new sound formats work without rewriting web pages.

sections.title: Security and Local Functions
sections.content:
Security of web real-time communication comes in three pieces: security of the components (browsers and servers, with the browser probably the most target-rich), security of the communication channels (participants should be able to verify the crypto parameters), and security of the partners' identities (verifying who they are, or keeping identities hidden when anonymity is a goal). The analysis and resulting requirements are in RFC 8826.

For local system functions such as echo cancellation, volume control and camera management, the exact algorithm need not be coordinated, though quality strongly affects user experience. The RFC says privacy concerns MUST be satisfied: if remote control of a camera is offered, the local participant should be able to find out who is controlling it and possibly revoke permission.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: You should always be able to tell who can see and hear you, and to say no. The browser and your computer handle that part.
